t: Are You Giving Out Lots Of Warnings? Here’s How To Fix It ow-to-fix-it/
q: Over and over readers asked us what they could do to limit the number of warnings they’re giving out.
Providing that the great majority of your students are heeding this initial consequence and not progressing to the next, it’s an indication that they’re taking your warnings as they’re intended.
The reason you’re giving out so many warnings is not because your students are taking advantage of them. The reason is because the purpose of the rule being broken isn’t embedded deep enough.
You have to create an experience through which they can feel the frustration of being on the receiving end of their disruptions.
Only by seeing themselves as others see them will things change. Only by identifying with the exasperation of others will they understand the true purpose of the rule.

t: Are You Humiliating Students Without Even Knowing it? knowing-it/
q: They are comments that roll off the tongue without second thought.
You see, what we may innocently describe as a way to shake a quixotic student into reality is actually one of the most hurtful and humiliating things you can ever do to them.
We forget that our students represent a kaleidoscope of different perspectives and sensibilities.
The humiliation of having an idea dismissed out of hand was brought home for me in a small way this past week. You see, I was on the other end of someone’s incredulity, and it hurt. It really did.
And the more heart and soul and thought that goes into an idea, the more destructive such reactions can be. It makes the person on the receiving end feel . . . well, stupid.
When you don’t take their ideas, questions, and curiosities seriously, you don’t take them seriously. And every time you dismiss their thinking as foolish, they grow a bit more jaded and demoralized.

Reflexive dismissive reactions to unusual student questions or ideas (e.g., "Why on earth would you want to do that?") can feel harmless to adults but are deeply humiliating to students.
Teachers often forget that students carry a wide range of personal perspectives and sensitivities shaped by their own experiences.
Dismissing a student's earnestly offered idea can make them feel demoralized and gradually erode their willingness to share and their sense of possibility.

The recommendation is not unconditional agreement, but taking students' ideas and questions seriously and protecting their dignity in every response.

t: Should Students Raise Their Hand In Small Groups? https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2015/02/14/should-students-raise-their-hand-in-small-groups/
q: Requiring students to raise their hand before speaking is good classroom management practice.
The truth is, with groups this size, it’s best to shelve the practice.
Asking students to raise their hand takes the joy out of being in a small group. It removes the essence, the seasoning, the élan of debate and discussion.
Your students must be able to speak directly to fellow group members without going through you first. Otherwise, they’ll grow bored with the process.
Another important goal should be to become less and less involved, to raise questions or advance ideas and then fade into the background.
Before jumping into small groups it’s important to model in detail what productive conversation looks like, including how to make eye contact, ask polite questions, and chime in without interrupting.

q: We teachers don't have enough time in our days; we can't just be doing things like writing #loveteaching posts if it's nothing more than a cute Valentine's Week activity. But it is way more than cute. Gary's idea is solid because the act of focusing on what we love about teaching is like doing a gratitude push-up; it strengthens the mental habit (or character strength) of appreciating what we've got and expressing that appreciation.

A big reason that I love teaching is that there's still this kid in me that thinks potential surrounds us — potential we can't even imagine. I think that even our most broken or withdrawn students can one day, like the Narnian trees, dazzle us. That potential is in them.

By habitually reigning in our focus, turning it from what we can't control to what we can, there's a teacher or two (or more) in every school in the country who is somehow flourishing during even this dark time for the teacher profession. We remind ourselves daily that, while our work is Never Finished, that's not necessarily a bad thing.

I'm the kind of person who doesn't long for a job where you can just be done improving; I don't want that. This is part of the reason I don't fret over evaluation scores and other external measures of my effectiveness. I don't care if I get an A on my evaluation; I do care about whether I've mastered more teaching at the end of this week than I had at the end of last week.

If I tell my students that grades are an important thing in one's life preparation but not the ultimate thing, then I, too, need to live the truth out. Grades do matter in the world we live in, and they can, in some ways, be of use to a learner.

My goodness — just writing those questions makes me want to write thousands more words. This is the good stuff, my friends. Cultivate this drive in yourself that isn't about points, but instead is about questions.

The key for me is always that the baby can't be thrown out with the bathwater. Self-control, grit, perseverance: these things do matter, for both our students and ourselves. Yet joy, humor, unrestrained curiosity — these are important, too.

t: Why You Should Never Give Choices Instead Of Consequences -of-consequences/
q: One of the more perplexing trends in classroom management is to give students choices instead of consequences.
The idea is to remove the source of his discontentment, to entice him with alternatives so that he will no longer engage in unwanted behavior.

When you appease difficult students by lowering academic or behavioral standards, you send an unmistakable message that they can complain, disrupt, and misbehave their way out of anything they deem unpleasant.

By giving in so readily, even voluntarily, you’re essentially telling them that you believe they’re incapable of changing their behavior. This is a form of labeling, and it is devastating to difficult students.

Letting students off the hook is akin to telling them they’re not good enough or worthy enough to be held to a higher standard, which strips away dignity and self-confidence faster and more effectively than yelling, sarcasm, or any other harmful method.
You follow your classroom management plan. You let accountability and your undying belief in them do their good work.
x: Linsin's alternative is unambiguous: follow the classroom management plan and give consequences, framing consistent accountability as an expression of belief in students' capability rather than punishment.
Michael Linsin sharply criticizes the trend of offering misbehaving students appealing alternatives (working on the rug, using an iPad, taking a break) instead of enforcing a warranted consequence.
It implicitly labels students as incapable of behavioral change, a label Linsin argues is devastating and self-fulfilling for difficult students.

He lists ten specific harms of this approach, including reinforcing entitlement, damaging trust with the rest of the class, and stripping students of dignity more effectively than yelling or sarcasm would.
The recommended alternative is straightforward: follow the classroom management plan and issue consequences, framed as an expression of belief in students' capability rather than punishment.
